RagShortTexts: The heraldic rule of tincture barred metal on metal, ensuring shields remained recognizable.

Variants.Content: As enclosed great helms concealed knightly faces, heraldry became an exact science of feudal identification. Heralds enforced the Rule of Tincture: metal (Or/Argent) must not be placed upon metal, nor colour (Gules, Azure, Sable, Vert, Purpure) upon colour. Armorial rolls recorded paternal lineages, cadency marks for younger sons, and banner designs.

The lion, fleur-de-lis, or eagle blazoned on a heater shield reflects ancestral blood spilled in holy enterprise. Usurping another's bearings invites trial before heraldic courts, public breaking of swords, and forfeiture of claims.

Amidst blood and dust, a soldier looks for the contrasting colors on lances and caparisons. When the golden leopard banner advances, you push forward; if the azure fleur-de-lis drops, order has collapsed.
